title: Enabling Hybrid HPCQC Workflows with a Heterogeneous Software Stack
authors: Muhammad Nufail Farooqi, Minh Chung, Burak Mete, Eric Mansfield, Bernd Hoffmann, Teemu Mattsson, Laura Schulz, Jorge Echavarria
abstract: In this work, we demonstrate hybrid High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) workflows on a production petascale system. The demonstration combines three components: the SuperMUC-NG supercomputer at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ), a 20-qubit superconducting quantum processor provided by IQM Quantum Computers (IQM), and Munich Quantum Valley (MQV)'s Munich Quantum Software Stack (MQSS).   Integrating quantum processors into High Performance Computing (HPC) systems requires a heterogeneous software stack capable of orchestrating classical and quantum resources within established supercomputing workflows. MQSS treats Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) as scheduler-managed accelerators and it performs resource coordination following a two-level scheduling scheme. Slurm performs system-level allocation by exposing QPUs as Generic RESources (GRES), while the MQSS Quantum Resource Manager & Compiler Infrastructure (QRM&CI) performs just-in-time compilation and subsequent dispatch of quantum circuits.   To integrate with existing HPC operations without modifying the scheduler core, MQSS introduces an open-source SLURM Plugin Suite based on Prolog/Epilog scripts and SPANK modules. Experimental results show that hybrid HPCQC workflows can be executed without significant latency overhead compared to conventional workloads.   The presented architecture provides a portable integration model for quantum accelerators on large-scale HPC systems and is directly applicable to next-generation Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Cray platforms, including LRZ's upcoming 'Blue Lion' supercomputer.
summary: This paper presents an architecture to enable hybrid High Performance Computing and Quantum Computing (HPCQC) workflows on large-scale supercomputers. It achieves this using a heterogeneous software stack that integrates the QPU into existing schedulers like SLURM by treating it as a managed accelerator. The successful demonstration proves that quantum resources can be incorporated with minimal performance overhead, paving the way for practical quantum acceleration in national labs.
main_problem: The core challenge is integrating Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) into existing, established High Performance Computing (HPC) supercomputing workflows.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated hybrid HPCQC workflows on a production petascale system with negligible latency overhead compared to purely classical workloads.
method: They developed and implemented a heterogeneous software stack featuring a two-level scheduling model orchestrated by an open-source SLURM Plugin Suite.
model_or_system: The system combines the SuperMUC-NG supercomputer, a 20-qubit superconducting QPU from IQM, and the Munich Quantum Software Stack (MQSS). This architecture treats QPUs as scheduler-managed accelerators.
key_observables: Latency overhead for hybrid jobs, average circuit runtimes for QAOA/VQE benchmarks, and real-time QPU status metrics like fidelity and calibration status.
important_parameters: The system operates on a petascale scale, utilizing 20 superconducting qubits, and employs SLURM's GRES mechanism for resource reservation.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that treating QPUs as scheduler-managed Generic Resources (GRES) is feasible without modifying the core scheduler logic. It also notes limitations regarding joint optimization of classical/quantum resources.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MQSS architecture, detailing the flow from front-end adapters through the QRM&CI to the quantum device, and show job pipeline examples within SLURM context.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity for integration, presents the two-level scheduling model (SLURM at Level 1, QRM&CI at Level 2), describes the implementation via plugins, and validates performance using benchmark measurements.
why_interesting: While focused on software infrastructure rather than fundamental physics, the work directly addresses the operationalization of quantum hardware by providing a robust, standardized interface layer necessary for any future experimental study in AMO or open quantum systems.
